AI Foundations for Managers · Final project · Yale SOM · October 2026

Home Turf

AI agents that find where your team's fan club watches the game in any city, verify it against the source, and help fan clubs and bars team up for the season, rivalry days included.

2. Motivation

Who has this problem. Fans who don't live where their team plays, and the volunteers who organize them. In one survey, only 36% of Americans who follow a sport live in the city where their favorite team plays, so roughly two in three don't.1 For some teams it's extreme: an analysis of geotagged posts found that 68% of Steelers fans live outside Pennsylvania.2 Those fans organize. The Buffalo Bills Backers grew to almost 500 chapters in 40+ states and 11 countries,3 Notre Dame has about 225 US clubs plus nearly 50 abroad,4 and USC is launching 20 Regional Trojan Networks.5 Game day is also big business for bars: 18.2 million Americans planned to watch the 2026 Super Bowl at a bar or restaurant.6

How they deal with it today. Three people are involved, and each has a different headache:

  • The traveling or transplanted fan Googles “USC bar Chicago”, sifts Reddit threads and fan blogs of unknown age, and often can't tell whether a listing is current. Team bar maps exist for a few NFL teams, but each covers only one team, and bars list themselves.
  • The club president (a volunteer) finds and vets a bar every season. USC's alumni association requires watch-party hosts to find a venue with “TVs with sound and the proper networks,” no deposit, and no food-and-beverage minimum, ideally the same venue every week.7 A Bills Backers leader in Baltimore said it “took us years to find like a spot that wasn't closing down or wasn't changing names.”3 Two clubs booked at the same bar can collide when their games overlap and only one can have the sound on.
  • The bar wants a 70-person club filling the room every Saturday of the season, but has no channel to reach the clubs except word of mouth.

What it costs them. For the fan: a wasted trip to a bar where the game isn't on, or with the sound on for someone else's team. For the president: hours of calls and visits each season, with no tool that checks schedule clashes. For the bar: empty seats on slow afternoons that a club would fill. One real example Home Turf's own agents surfaced: the Harvard and Yale clubs of Chicago both list the same bar for their 2026 Harvard–Yale viewing party, coordinated by hand on two separate club websites (Fig. 5).

3. What is new here

I looked at 14 existing products and sources: Steelers Nation Unite, PackersEverywhere, Bills Backers, Browns Backers, USC, Notre Dame, and Harvard/Yale club pages, FANZO (MatchPint), DIRECTV Sports Bar Finder, CrowdKick, Yelp, Google Maps, Reddit, Meetup, Eventbrite, Peerspace, and ChatGPT/Perplexity search. The pieces exist, but they're scattered across team sites, school sites, and general apps, and none of them verifies what it shows or coordinates the people involved.

Existing optionWhat it's good atWhat it lacks
Team bar finders (Steelers Nation Unite, PackersEverywhere, Bills Backers map, Browns Backer Tracker)Official, map-basedOne team each; bars self-list with no verification; no planning tools
Alumni association game-watch pages (USC, Notre Dame, Harvard/Yale clubs)Authoritative for that schoolOne school, one event at a time; hosts still find and vet bars by hand
FANZO (formerly MatchPint), DIRECTV Sports Bar FinderWhich venue shows which gameBuilt around fixtures, not fan communities; DIRECTV says it can't guarantee a game is shown
Yelp, Google Maps, Reddit, local news listsBroad coverageDon't know which bar hosts which club; information goes stale
Meetup, Eventbrite, PeerspaceRSVPs and venue bookingBuilt for one-off events, not season-long club and bar deals
ChatGPT or Perplexity web searchAnswers any team and cityNo verification layer; AI search tools were wrong on over 60% of citation queries (Tow Center, 2025)
Home TurfAny team, any city, verified; clubs and bars on one platformNeeds bars and clubs to join (cold start)

What Home Turf does differently. (1) Any team, any city, one search, instead of one team's map or one school's page, and a city view that shows every team's logo where its fans gather, filterable by league. (2) Verification as a feature: every spot is re-checked by code against its source, labeled Verified, Likely, or Unverified, and shown with the quote and link, so a fan can judge freshness. This addresses the specific weakness of plain AI search, which confidently cites wrong or stale pages. (3) A two-sided marketplace with planning agents: the Season Matchmaker ranks bars for a club and computes schedule clashes with other clubs at the same bar; the rivalry planner builds a joint watch party for two rival clubs at a neutral bar; bars pitch clubs with a writer that cannot promise anything their profile doesn't support. I didn't find any product that does (3). Honest caveat: the official team and alumni pages are more authoritative than Home Turf for their own team. Home Turf treats them as its best sources rather than competing with them.

4. The agents

AgentWhat it doesToolsSettings
RouterTurns “Bears fans in Boston” (or just “Boston”) into intent, team, city; declines off-topic or unsafe requestsNoneeffort none; cached 30 days
ScoutFinds where fans or the official club watch: bar, street address, club, source URL, exact quote, season. If nothing usable turns up, a wide second pass searches the metro area and fan club directories and returns verified “shows every game” best betsOpenAI web_searchmax 3 searches, then max 4 only if needed
City SweepMaps many teams' fan bars in one city at once (NFL, college, other leagues) so the city map shows every team's logo; results become per-team cache entriesweb_searchmax 4 per league group; one batched verification
ReputationA real bar's public ratings and review themes, summarized in its own words with links out; photos from the bar's own websiteweb_search, site_photosmax 2 searches; cached 30 days
VerifierRe-checks each candidate: geocodes the address, re-opens the source, looks for the bar's name and the current season. Model only for unclear cases, in one batched callfetch_page, geocode (OpenStreetMap)code first; effort low
ScheduleA team's season schedule (date, opponent, kickoff, TV)web_searchmax 2 searches; cached 24 h
MatchmakerSeason mode: ranks bars for a club, explains clashes. Rivalry mode: one bar for two rival clubs, logistics, three draftsProfiles, schedules, conflicts computed in codeonly candidate bar_ids accepted
Pitch WriterDrafts a bar's invitation to a club from the bar's profile onlyProfile facts; number validatorone retry if a number is invented
GuardScreens reviews, profiles, pitches for injection, spam, abuse, personal info, false claimsFree code filter, then modelfails closed
SummarizerTurns posted reviews into a game-day score (TVs, sound, crowd, service)Nonecached by review hash

How they're organized. Not a free-roaming “boss” agent: each user action runs a fixed pipeline, which is cheaper, easier to test, and can't loop. A search is Router → (cache) → Scout → Verifier. A rivalry plan is Schedule → code facts → Matchmaker → human approvals. Hand-offs happen in code through typed Pydantic objects, so each agent gets only what it needs. Agents never get tools that commit anything; the only commitment buttons (choose a home bar, approve a watch party, send a pitch) are clicked by people.

Model choice. All agents use gpt-6-luna (course key: $0.10 per 1M input tokens, $0.50 per 1M output). The work is short, structured, and grounded in retrieved text, which suits a small, cheap model. I varied reasoning effort per agent rather than the model: “none” for Router and Summarizer, “low” elsewhere. I tested “medium” effort for the Scout (Section 5): it cost 25% more without finding more verified spots.

One real run, step by step: “Seattle Seahawks fans in Denver”

  1. Router: find: Seattle Seahawks in Denver, CO, parsed instantly against the team table, so no model call. Not in the cache, so the Scout runs.
  2. Scout runs two web searches and returns two candidates with addresses, quotes, and sources: Rhein Haus Denver (1415 Market St) and Clock Tower Grill. It also finds the official club, the Rocky Mountain Sea Hawkers.
  3. Verifier re-opens each source. For Rhein Haus the page names the bar and mentions 2026, so free code settles it (“It's the official home of the Mile High Sea Hawkers”). The other goes to the model in one batched call and comes back Likely.
  4. Result: a large Seahawks logo pin for each spot, ringed green (Verified) or amber (Likely), on a Denver map that also shows the Steelers bars already known in the city. The run receipt: 2 AI calls, 16,597 input tokens (5,311 cached), 553 output, 2 web searches, 5.8 s, $0.0215.

The city view: every team's logo on one map

Search just “Chicago” (or click a city) and the map shows every team whose fans have a known spot there, each pin a team logo ringed in its verification color, with bars that host several clubs showing several logos. League buttons filter the map to NFL, NCAA, MLB, NBA, NHL, or Soccer. The data comes from cached verified searches, the City Sweep agent (which reads city-wide guides such as “a bar for every NFL team” and alumni watch-party listings), fan suggestions, and partner bars. A sweep costs about $0.09 per city and adds roughly 15 teams; after that, every team search in that city is free.

The marketplace run: a Harvard–Yale watch party in Chicago

Logged in as the (demo) Yale club president, one click runs Schedule (from cache) → code facts → Matchmaker. The schedule shows The Game on Nov 21 at 3:30 PM ET on ESPNU. Code computes the combined turnout (85) and which bars can hold it, then the Matchmaker ranks four, recommends neutral Fullerton Field House (holds 240, two rooms with separate sound), and drafts three invitations. Nothing is sent: the proposing president's approval is recorded, then the bar and the Harvard president each approve from their own dashboards (Fig. 7). The whole plan cost $0.0007.

5. Tokenomics

All numbers below come from the app's own usage log, recorded on 2026-10-24 by scripts/measure_tokens.py (raw data: docs/measurements.json). Every model call records input, cached-input, output, and reasoning tokens, web searches, latency, and cost. The public site keeps this out of sight; in operator mode (HOME_TURF_OPS=1) every result shows its receipt (Fig. 3), and the operator console at /admin totals everything (Fig. 12).

The surprise: tokens are cheap, web searches aren't. A new search averages 14,899 input tokens, of which 5,245 were cached, plus 578 output (182 of them reasoning). Those tokens cost only about $0.0013. The web-search fee ($0.01 per call, 1.25 calls on average) is $0.0125, or 90% of the cost. So the lever that matters is avoiding repeat web searches, not trimming prompts.

Cost per user per month, and at scale

Usage assumptions (mine, stated so they can be challenged): fans make 6 searches a month, presidents 8 searches plus one season match and one rivalry plan, bars 4 searches and 4 pitches. The cache hit rate is the key unknown. In a small pilot, most searches are new (30% hits assumed). At 10,000 users, popular pairs like “Bears fans in Boston” repeat constantly, and there are only a few thousand realistic team + city pairs, each refreshed at most weekly, so 85% is a reasonable estimate.

At 10,000 users the AI bill is about $136.54 a month, about 1.4 cents per user, which a single bar subscription would cover many times over. Hosting would cost more than the AI. Note that the app's built-in daily cap (3M tokens, about 190 new searches a day) is sized for a class pilot and would be raised for a real launch.

Speed. After pilot feedback that search felt slow, I profiled a live search: Router 1–2 s, Scout web search 5–6 s, source re-checks and geocoding 1–2 s, Verifier 1.5 s, and the wide pass another 7.5 s when it ran. Three changes followed: plain searches (“Bears fans in Boston”, “Boston”) are parsed locally against the team table and skip the Router call; all source re-checks run in parallel; and the wide pass runs automatically only when nothing at all is found (otherwise the fan gets a “Search wider” button). Four fresh searches afterward took 5.8, 6.6, 9.0, and 18.6 s (the last one needed the wide pass), down from about 12 s typical. The Scout's web search is now the floor.

What I did to keep cost down

  1. Result cache (7 days). A repeat team + city costs $0 and under 0.1 s instead of $0.0138 and 12 s (measured: 8 of 8 repeats at $0). Seeded demo cities load instantly.
  2. Router cache (30 days) for identical searches, and schedule cache (24 h), so matchmaking and pitches reuse schedules (measured: 0 web searches in every matchmaker and pitch run).
  3. Code before model. The Verifier settled 8 of 18 candidates with free checks and sent the rest to the model in one batched call (about $0.0002). The Guard's regex layer blocks obvious injections with zero tokens. Matchmaker capacity and schedule-clash math are done in code.
  4. Hard limits. Max 3 web searches per Scout, 2 per Schedule lookup, at most 5 candidates verified, max output tokens per agent, and token caps per action, session, and day.
  5. Smallest effective reasoning. Effort “none” for Router and Summarizer, “low” elsewhere. Summaries are cached until a new review arrives.
  6. Prompt layout for caching. Static rules first, per-request data last. Honest finding: my own prompts (about 700–900 tokens) are below the 1,024-token minimum for OpenAI prompt caching, so they don't cache. The 5,245 cached tokens per search come from the web-search tool's own instructions, which repeat on every Scout call. Padding prompts to reach the threshold would cost more than it saves.

Did cutting cost make the app worse? An experiment

I ran the Scout and Verifier on the same 6 team + city searches with three settings:

SettingWeb searches usedSearches with a good spotGood spots / searchVerified spotsOfficial club foundCost / searchTime
production (low effort, max 3 searches)1.336/61.6765/6$0.01478.2 s
cheaper (low effort, max 1 search)1.176/61.6775/6$0.01297.6 s
pricier (medium effort, max 6 searches)1.676/62.3355/6$0.018411.4 s

Result. Capping the Scout at 1 search was 12% cheaper than production and found the same number of good spots, so the cut did not hurt on this sample. Spending more (medium effort, up to 6 searches) cost 26% more and found more candidates (2.33 vs 1.67 per search) but fewer verified ones (5 vs 6): extra searches pulled in weaker, less current sources. I kept the cap at 3 because the model only used 1.33 on average and harder searches (e.g., Notre Dame in Boston, where nothing could be verified) need the headroom. Caveats: 6 searches is a small sample, and production's times are understated because the Portkey gateway served some identical requests from its own cache.

A cost cut that did hurt, and the fix. The free code checks in the Verifier occasionally miss: when a source blocks automated fetches (HTTP 403), code can't confirm the spot, and the cheap fallback is to call it “Likely” on the strength of the Scout's quote. That is honest but less useful than a confirmation. Adding a second independent source fixes it: when two sources agree and one is official, code upgrades the spot to Verified (this is how USC's Chicago spot, Theory, is verified).

6. Safety

The risks that matter here are different from a generic chatbot: Home Turf reads untrusted web pages, publishes user content, and sits between businesses that have a reason to game it (a bar wants to rank first). The full rule list, with where each rule is enforced, is in docs/GUARDRAILS.md; every rule there traces to a lecture or homework from this course.

RiskDefense builtEvidenceResult
Prompt injection in reviews, profiles, pitchesFree regex layer, then Guard agent; untrusted text fenced as dataFig. 9, 10; testsBlocked
Injection inside a web page the Scout readsVerifier rejects any spot whose source contains instructions to AItest_verifier_rejects_injected_sourceBlocked
Agent invents a bar, address, or map locationEvery spot needs a source + quote; code re-fetches the page; geocoder (not the model) places pinsFig. 4; 2 testsCaught
Matchmaker recommends a bar that doesn't exist or can't fitOnly candidate bar_ids accepted; capacity re-checked in codetest_matchmaker_drops_invented_barCaught
Bar pitch promises things the bar never offeredNumber validator (prices must match exactly) + Guard false-claim checkFig. 8Blocked
Agent takes a wrong action (books, sends, approves)No agent has those tools; people approve; rivalry needs all 3 partiesFig. 7; test_event_needs_three_approvalsBy design
Model-supplied URL hits the host machine (SSRF)fetch_page allows public http(s) only; re-checks after redirectstest_private_urls_refusedBlocked
Runaway loop or abuse burns the budgetMax 3 searches per Scout; token caps per action, session, day; cachestest_run_budget_stops_runaway, test_daily_capCapped
Personal data exposedReviews with phone or email blocked; only public club and business contacts usedtest_phone_and_email_blockedBlocked
Off-topic use of the paid modelRouter declines non-sports requestsFig. 11Declined
Copying reviews or photos we don't ownReputation agent summarizes themes in its own words, reports ratings only if a source shows them, links out; photos and logos are linked from their ownersFig. 4e; GUARDRAILS S15By design
Fans submitting fake or malicious spotsSuggestions pass the Guard, are labeled Fan-suggested, and become Verified only if a linked page names the bar and teamtest_suggestion_with_injection_blockedBlocked
Script injection through map dataMap data JSON-escaped and HTML-escaped; maps served from our own origintest_map_escapes_script_breakoutBlocked

Automated tests. tests/test_safety.py has 22 tests: 19 offline (no API cost, stubbed model) covering injection, personal info, length caps, invented numbers, SSRF, run and daily caps, injected source pages, unmappable addresses, invented bars, three-party approval, schedule-clash math, logo and league matching, map escaping, and fan-suggestion screening; plus 3 live tests against gpt-6-luna (spam, false profile claims, off-topic search). All 22 pass, including from a fresh clone on Python 3.11.

Agent malfunction. The model never writes coordinates; a geocoder does. Every claim must carry a source and a quote, which code re-checks. Agent failures are contained: an exception becomes a polite message, the Guard fails closed (holds the post) if it can't reach the model, and a schedule failure lets matchmaking continue with a note. Overspending. Every call passes a budget check first (120k tokens per action, 600k per browser session, 3M per day app-wide), web searches are capped per agent, and the console shows live meters (Fig. 12). The audit trail (runtime/audit_log.jsonl) is append-only and records every agent call, tool call, Guard decision, and human approval, without secrets.

The bar's side, as an estimate

Illustrative only, with stated assumptions rather than sourced data: a club of 70 fans at a home bar for a 12-game season, spending an assumed $30 each per game, is $25,200 of revenue for the bar from one club, mostly on afternoons that would otherwise be slow. If a bar paid even $50 a month to be matched with clubs, one club would return that many times over, and Home Turf's AI cost per user is a fraction of a cent. Supporting evidence that game days move bar spending: restaurants' alcohol sales on NFL-season Sundays ran about 6% above off-season Sundays nationally in Toast's 2023 point-of-sale data (and far higher in Green Bay).9

Something newly possible. The rivalry watch party: no tool today can take two rival clubs in a city, find the game in both schedules, pick a neutral bar that fits both crowds, and get three parties to sign off. Home Turf does it in one click and under a tenth of a cent.

8. Limits and next steps

What doesn't work yet.

  • Coverage depends on the web. Where no page ties a bar to a team (Falcons in Phoenix), Home Turf says so, offers verified “shows every game” bars, and asks fans to add the spot. Honest, but not the answer a fan hoped for.
  • No direct Yelp or Google review feed. Their APIs need keys this project can't require and their terms forbid scraping, so review themes are summarized from public pages and the Google card is an embed.
  • Some sources block re-checking (HTTP 403 or JavaScript-only pages), which caps those spots at Likely.
  • Schedules can disagree across sources (one source lists Packers–Bears as TBD, another as 1:00 PM ET); clash detection marks TBD overlaps as “possible.”
  • The marketplace is seeded. Bars, clubs, people, and seed reviews in the demo are fictional and labeled “demo.” Claiming a bar has no business verification yet, and logins are one-click demo accounts.
  • Real-user evidence is from a small pilot (see Section 7), not a bar or club that has run a season on it.
  • My own prompts are too short to use prompt caching, and the per-day cap is sized for a pilot.

With another month.

  1. Onboard real supply: invite 5 bars and 5 alumni or fan clubs in one city (Chicago or Boston), with business verification for bar claims and real accounts (the HW4 PBKDF2 login pattern).
  2. Post-game confirmations: after each game, ask attendees “was the club here, was the sound on?”. This turns fans into the verification layer and keeps data fresh.
  3. Real messaging with approval: send drafted invitations by email only after the human clicks send, reusing the Outlook MCP pattern from Lecture 9.
  4. Adaptive Scout: start with 1 web search and escalate only when nothing verifies, which the experiment suggests cuts cost about 12% without losing quality.
  5. Hosting and mobile: a hosted version with a mobile layout for fans standing on a sidewalk in a new city.
  6. MCP distribution (already prototyped in mcp_server/): let fans and presidents ask their own assistant “where do Bills fans watch in Denver?”.
